piezas.titulo: Why Role-Based Access Control Fails for AI Agents — and How to Fix It With Memory Lineage Engines
piezas.resumenOriginal: Key Takeaways Role-based access control (RBAC) and content-tagging systems check whether a requester's credentials match a label attached to data . That check has nothing to say about a derived, cached result — a plain number with no tag of its own. A cached metric like churn_rate = 0.114 can be computed from a query that touches a restricted column ( income ) and then be served to a department that was never allowed to see that column, without a single existing access control catching it. The fix is to gate retrieval on the result's derivation graph — the tables, columns, and filters that produced it — rather than on a tag attached after the fact. In benchmark testing, this reduced a structural cross-department leak rate of 18.8%–25.5% to zero, at a real, measurable cost: roughly 13 additional query executions per 100 requests, and a gate-check predicate costing 0.09 microseconds. The mechanism does not stop inference attacks, a compromised memory store, or collusion — it closes one specific, previously unguarded gap in agent-memory retrieval. A Clean Integer That Still Leaks a Restricted Column Take a concrete scenario. A Finance agent runs a query that joins a transactions table against a customer_pii table — which includes an income column — to compute a churn_rate for customers who have gone quiet in the last 90 days. It gets back a single float: 0.114 . Nothing about that number looks sensitive. No names, no account numbers, no raw income figures. The agent caches the result in shared memory so the next agent that asks for churn_rate does not have to recompute it. A week later, a Marketing agent asks the same shared memory for churn_rate and gets 0.114 back instantly, with no query executed. Marketing was never granted access to income . Its role-based access-control (RBAC) entry explicitly blocks that column. But nothing in this transaction touched income directly — Marketing did not query the column, did not see a row containing it, and did not request anything with "income" in the name. It asked for a key performance indicator (KPI) by name and got a float back.

piezas.titulo: Penetrating needling from Qiuxu (GB40) to Zhaohai (KI6) versus separate needling for post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction: an assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial protocol
piezas.resumenOriginal: Post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction limits mobility, balance, and independence and remains a major target of neurorehabilitation. Acupuncture is widely used as an adjunctive intervention after stroke, but direct randomized evidence comparing penetrating needling with conventional separate needling at the same acupoints is limited. This protocol describes an active-comparator randomized controlled trial comparing penetrating needling from Qiuxu (GB40) to Zhaohai (KI6) with separate needling for post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction, with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and surface electromyography (sEMG) included as exploratory mechanistic outcomes. This single-center, prospective, assessor-blinded, parallel-group superiority trial will enroll 130 participants with subacute post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to penetrating needling from Qiuxu (GB40) to Zhaohai (KI6) or to separate needling at the same acupoints. Both groups will receive 12 acupuncture sessions over 2 weeks, delivered 6 times per week, with 30 min of needle retention per session, together with the same total rehabilitation dose of 30 min/day, 5 days/week. The primary outcome is the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Lower Extremity (FMA-LE) score at the end of treatment (T1). The primary analysis will use analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline FMA-LE. Secondary clinical outcomes include the Berg Balance Scale, Manual Muscle Testing, and Modified Ashworth Scale. Registered secondary neurophysiological assessments include fNIRS and sEMG; their derived measures will be analyzed exploratorily.Clinical trial registrationhttps://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn/mgt/project/view/2037483478790045696, ITMCTR2026000773.

piezas.titulo: State-dependent responses of emotional brain networks in high myopia under blurred vision: a shift towards dorsal stream and cross-modal processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: PurposeReliable sensory input plays a vital role in shaping emotional experience, however, how the brain modulates the formation of emotion under chronic visual degradation remains unclear. Using high myopia (HM) as a natural model of sustained blur, this study investigated state-dependent responses of emotional brain networks during blurred movie viewing.MethodsTwenty-four participants with high myopia (HM) were tested without optical correction, comparing with normal vision (NV) controls from previous research. All participants watched thriller and scenic movie clips twice over one week during fMRI. Intra-subject synchrony and seed-based functional connectivity analyses focused on the amygdala and visual processing streams.ResultsCompared to NV controls, the HM group exhibited reduced intra-subject synchrony in visual cortices but increased synchrony in the primary auditory cortex, indicating cross-modal compensatory enhancement. During threat processing, HM participants showed strengthened and stable functional connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsal visual stream. For non-threatening content, this enhanced connectivity initially involved both dorsal and ventral stream but persisted selectively in the dorsal stream upon repeated viewing.ConclusionSustained visual blur elicits a perceptual-state-dependent functional response in emotional networks, characterized by heightened cross-modal auditory integration and an increased recruitment of the visual dorsal stream during blurred viewing. These findings highlight the brain’s immediate compensatory mechanisms under conditions of ambiguous visual input.

piezas.titulo: Repetitive suprathreshold paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation alters corticospinal excitability
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background: Suprathreshold paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) at interstimulus intervals (ISIs) of 20-30 ms evokes cumulative online increases in corticospinal excitability. Whether these changes persist beyond stimulation remains unclear. This study investigated whether repetitive paired-pulse TMS targeting periods of net excitation or inhibition induces offline changes in corticospinal excitability. Methods: Nineteen healthy participants completed three sessions, separated by at least one week, involving 40 pairs of repetitive paired-pulse TMS delivered to the left primary motor cortex at an ISI of 20 ms (rPPS20) or 100 ms (rPPS100), or a single-pulse control condition (rSPS). Offline changes in corticospinal excitability were assessed using motor evoked potential (MEP) amplitudes recorded before and after stimulation. Results: During stimulation, MEP amplitudes decreased across trials in the rPPS100 condition, although online changes did not differ significantly between conditions. Following stimulation, MEP amplitudes were significantly reduced for up to 40 minutes after rPPS100 (p = 0.017) but were not changed following rPPS20 or rSPS (all p > 0.05). Conclusion: Contrary to our hypothesis, repetitive paired-pulse TMS targeting periods of net excitation did not induce offline changes in corticospinal excitability. In contrast, stimulation targeting long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) produced sustained reductions in corticospinal excitability, suggesting that repetitive LICI-inducing stimulation can induce lasting plasticity within the corticospinal system.

piezas.titulo: Treatment Fidelity of AquOTic: An Occupational Therapy-Based Aquatic Intervention for Children on the Autism Spectrum.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceChildren on the autism spectrum face significantly higher risks for unintentional drowning, yet aquatic interventions often lack the standardized specification necessary for evidence-based replication.ObjectiveTo examine the treatment fidelity of AquOTic.DesignDescriptive design based on a larger randomized controlled trial.SettingCounty Board of Developmental Disabilities therapy pool.ParticipantsChildren on the autism spectrum (N = 37) ages 5 to 9 year and graduate-level therapy students (swim buddies, N = 18).InterventionAquOTic is a manualized 10-week occupational therapy-based water competency intervention for children on the autism spectrum.Outcomes and MeasuresAdherence was measured via a 13-item fidelity self-checklist and video-coding analysis.ResultsHigh overall fidelity was achieved, with mean swim buddy adherence at 95.93%. Component-level fidelity averaged 97.36%, with core ingredients such as play-based strategies, modeling, and water property integration consistently appearing in 100% of analyzed sessions.Conclusions and RelevanceThe AquOTic intervention demonstrates high treatment fidelity, confirming that theorized active ingredients are consistently implemented. Use of fidelity practices and intervention specification supports the reproducibility and clinical translation of occupational therapy-led aquatic interventions to improve water safety for autistic children.

piezas.titulo: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
piezas.resumenOriginal: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. La empresa diseñó Scion, su propio sistema de control de versiones, para manejar cientos de gigabytes de historial y millones de descargas diarias. El equipo de siete personas completó la migración en cinco meses, lo que sugiere que la nueva arquitectura permite escalar sin los cuellos de botella de Git.
